lessonTitle: Analgesic Titration, Symptom Management and Palliative Emergencies

blocks.text: Mr Shaw, 71, has bone metastases from prostate cancer. His pain was controlled on modified-release morphine, but over three days he has needed the 'as required' dose six times a day and now has constipation, nausea and drowsiness. Last night he developed new back pain and his legs felt 'heavy'. Which of these problems is a routine titration issue, and which one cannot wait until morning?

blocks.markdown: Symptom control in advanced illness follows a few reliable principles: **assess the cause and mechanism**, **explain and agree a plan with the patient**, treat reversible contributors, use **simple, regular, individualised** drug regimens by the least invasive effective route, **titrate** to effect, **review** often, and anticipate predictable problems. Most advice in this unit comes from NICE guidance on opioids in palliative care (CG140), NICE guidance on care of dying adults and end of life care (NG31, NG142), the BNF and the **Palliative Care Formulary (PCF)**. All doses in this unit are teaching examples and must be checked against the current BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance; specialist palliative care advice should be sought whenever there is doubt, renal impairment or complex symptoms.

blocks.title: Breakthrough dose and the 24-hour total
blocks.text: The **24-hour opioid total** is the sum of the regular opioid taken over 24 hours (plus any extra breakthrough doses actually used). A **breakthrough dose** is an immediate-release dose of the same opioid, given as needed for pain that breaks through regular analgesia. It is typically calculated as roughly **one-sixth of the total 24-hour dose** (many references allow a range from one-tenth to one-sixth, depending on the patient and clinician judgement; check local guidance). **Titration** means adjusting the regular dose according to the response and use of breakthrough doses, usually daily at first.

blocks.markdown: **Analgesic titration for cancer pain (objective 1).** Assess pain by site, character, severity, mechanism (nociceptive, visceral, neuropathic, bone), and its effect on function and mood. The WHO analgesic ladder (non-opioid, weak opioid, strong opioid, each with adjuvants) remains a guide, and guidance for patients needing a strong opioid is to start with oral morphine, either modified-release or immediate-release titrated, with immediate-release breakthrough doses, and to adjust the regular dose by reviewing 24-hour use. Each opioid prescription should be accompanied by: a regular **laxative** (opioid-induced constipation is expected and not tolerance-limited), advice and an as-required antiemetic if nausea occurs, and warnings about drowsiness (which usually settles within days). Neuropathic pain may require adjuvant drugs, bone pain may respond to radiotherapy, NSAIDs or bisphosphonates according to the situation, and spasm or visceral pain may need antispasmodics. **Renal impairment:** morphine has active metabolites (such as morphine-6-glucuronide) that accumulate when kidney function is reduced, causing sedation, myoclonus or toxicity. In moderate to severe renal impairment, a different opioid such as oxycodone (with caution and dose reduction) or alfentanil (often by subcutaneous infusion) may be chosen on specialist or PCF advice. Opioid switching also needs care: **cross-tolerance is incomplete**, so conversion ratios are approximate, often with a cautious reduction in the calculated dose of the new opioid, and the patient needs close review. Never rely on one conversion table alone.

blocks.caption: Breakthrough dose as a fraction of the 24-hour opioid total, in the same drug and the same route; check the range against local policy, the BNF and the Palliative Care Formulary. Round to practical doses.

blocks.title: Calculating breakthrough from regular morphine
blocks.prompt: Mr Shaw takes modified-release oral morphine 30 mg twice daily. Calculate the 24-hour dose and a suitable breakthrough dose range using the one-tenth to one-sixth rule. (Teaching example only: check against the current BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance.)

steps.text: Total 24-hour oral morphine: 30 mg x 2 = 60 mg.

State the range: about 6 mg to 10 mg of immediate-release oral morphine per breakthrough dose; clinicians commonly choose 10 mg for practicality, adjusting for frailty and renal function, and reviewing efficacy and side effects.
Safety: confirm renal function, check the dose against current references, and review after 24 hours. If he is using more than about two or three breakthrough doses daily, titrate the regular dose.

blocks.answer: The 24-hour total is 60 mg and the breakthrough range is about 6 to 10 mg of oral immediate-release morphine.

blocks.title: Converting to a subcutaneous infusion
blocks.prompt: Mr Shaw can no longer swallow. Over 24 hours he used regular morphine 60 mg orally plus three 10 mg breakthrough doses. Using an oral-to-subcutaneous morphine ratio of 2 to 1, calculate a 24-hour subcutaneous morphine dose and a breakthrough dose range. (Teaching example only: check against current references; seek specialist advice if renal impairment or unsure.)

steps.text: Total oral morphine used in 24 hours: 60 mg + (3 x 10 mg) = 90 mg.
Convert to subcutaneous morphine by dividing by 2, since subcutaneous morphine is about twice as potent as oral: 90 / 2 = 45 mg over 24 hours.
Calculate the subcutaneous breakthrough dose range: 45 / 6 = 7.5 mg and 45 / 10 = 4.5 mg.

Check the plan: confirm renal function (if impaired, morphine may accumulate and an alternative such as alfentanil may be preferred after specialist advice), prescribe an anti-emetic and other anticipatory medicines, and review pain and sedation at least daily.
Remember limitations: ratios are approximate, and an opioid that has been switched needs close monitoring for both under- and over-treatment.

blocks.answer: The 45 mg subcutaneous 24-hour dose from 90 mg oral, with breakthrough doses of about 4.5 to 7.5 mg subcutaneously, subject to checking against current references.

blocks.markdown:
**Other symptoms (objective 2).** Always assess and treat reversible causes, use non-drug measures, and choose drugs for the likely mechanism.

- **Breathlessness:** treat reversible causes (infection, effusion, anaemia, heart failure, bronchospasm), use a handheld fan, positioning, breathing control and pacing, and explain and reassure. Low-dose opioids can reduce the sensation of breathlessness, and a benzodiazepine may help if anxiety is prominent; use oxygen only for demonstrated hypoxaemia. Check doses against current references.
- **Nausea and vomiting:** choose the antiemetic by cause (see table).
- **Constipation:** prescribe a regular stimulant laxative, often with a softener, with every strong opioid; check for impaction and obstruction before escalating; review other constipating drugs.
- **Agitation and terminal restlessness:** search for reversible causes (pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, drugs, metabolic disturbance), use calm environment and reassurance, and if drugs are needed use a symptom-directed agent such as haloperidol for delirium or midazolam for anxiety or distress, with doses taken from current references.

rows: Gastric stasis or functional obstruction (early satiety, hiccup)
Avoid in complete mechanical bowel obstruction; check dose and renal function
QT prolongation and extrapyramidal effects; low doses; check interactions
Raised intracranial pressure, vestibular or some mechanical bowel obstruction
Anticholinergic effects; caution in heart failure and with other anticholinergics
Sedation and hypotension; specialist advice often useful
blocks.caption: Antiemetic choice by mechanism. Doses and details must be checked against the BNF and the Palliative Care Formulary.

blocks.markdown:
**Palliative emergencies (objective 3).** Recognise early, because prompt treatment preserves function and comfort, then decide with the patient and team whether active treatment is consistent with their goals.

- **Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC):** suspect in a patient with known cancer (for example prostate, breast, lung, myeloma) and new or worsening back pain, especially thoracic or band-like, pain on lying flat, leg weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel disturbance. Urgent specialist discussion, whole-spine MRI (NICE guidance NG234 sets timeframes, typically within 24 hours when there are neurological symptoms or signs), analgesia, dexamethasone according to local protocol, and care of the spine until stability is assessed.
- **Hypercalcaemia of malignancy:** thirst, polyuria, nausea, constipation, confusion and drowsiness. Measure the albumin-adjusted calcium, rehydrate with intravenous fluid, and consider a bisphosphonate according to local protocol and the person's goals.
- **Superior vena cava obstruction:** facial and arm swelling, dilated neck veins and breathlessness; urgent assessment and corticosteroids or stenting or radiotherapy as appropriate.
- **Massive haemorrhage, seizures and neutropenic sepsis:** have a plan, and 'crisis' medication prescribed when the risk is predictable.

Albumin-adjusted calcium (mmol/L) is commonly estimated as measured calcium plus 0.02 times the difference between 40 and the albumin in g/L; laboratories differ in the formula they use.

items: Review and titrate analgesia daily at first; count breakthrough doses and adjust the regular dose.
Prescribe a laxative with every opioid and an antiemetic available as needed.
Check renal function before choosing or converting an opioid; ask for specialist advice if impaired.
Treat reversible causes of dyspnoea, nausea and agitation and use non-drug measures.
Know the red flags for MSCC, hypercalcaemia and SVC obstruction and escalate urgently.

blocks.title: Mechanism, route, review
blocks.text: Match the drug to the mechanism, use the simplest effective route, titrate to effect using 24-hour use, and review frequently. Anticipate opioid adverse effects, especially constipation. Always verify doses, conversions and renal function against the BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance, and ask a palliative care team for advice when in doubt.

blocks.title: High-risk errors
blocks.text: Opioid conversions are approximate, cross-tolerance is incomplete and renal impairment alters opioid handling. Miscalculating the 24-hour total, confusing oral and subcutaneous doses, or mixing up morphine and diamorphine or oxycodone doses can be fatal. Double-check arithmetic, use two checkers, and never use a conversion from memory alone.

points: Titrate opioids against 24-hour use; breakthrough is roughly one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (range one-tenth to one-sixth), prescribe a laxative and review often.

Oral-to-subcutaneous morphine conversion is approximately 2 to 1; opioid switching is approximate because of incomplete cross-tolerance and renal impairment may favour alternatives on specialist advice.
Manage breathlessness, nausea, constipation and agitation by cause, with non-drug measures and symptom-directed drugs checked against current references.
Recognise palliative emergencies such as MSCC and hypercalcaemia early; hypercalcaemia is judged on albumin-adjusted calcium.

questions.stem: A patient with cancer pain takes regular modified-release oral morphine and uses several breakthrough doses daily. Which approach best reflects safe titration practice?

options.text: Double the regular dose without review
Stop the breakthrough dose to avoid opioid exposure
Review 24-hour use, adjust the regular dose accordingly, prescribe a regular laxative and review within a day or two
Avoid laxatives to keep the patient's bowel regimen simple

questions.correctOptionText: Review 24-hour use, adjust the regular dose accordingly, prescribe a regular laxative and review within a day or two

distractorRationale.b: Breakthrough dosing is a core part of titration.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: titration uses actual 24-hour use with safeguards and review.
distractorRationale.d: Opioid-induced constipation is predictable and needs prophylaxis.

questions.explanation: Titration relies on the total used in 24 hours, including breakthrough, and on regular review. Laxatives are prescribed with opioids because constipation is expected, and all doses are checked against current references.

questions.stem: A patient takes modified-release oral morphine 90 mg twice daily. Using one-sixth of the 24-hour dose, calculate a breakthrough dose of immediate-release oral morphine in mg (teaching example only; check against current BNF/Palliative Care Formulary).
questions.explanation: The 24-hour oral morphine dose is 90 x 2 = 180 mg, and one-sixth of 180 mg is 30 mg. Many references allow a range down to one-tenth (18 mg), so the final dose depends on judgement and local guidance.

questions.stem: A patient has used a total of 150 mg of oral morphine in 24 hours. Using an oral-to-subcutaneous morphine ratio of 2 to 1, what is the equivalent 24-hour subcutaneous morphine dose in mg (teaching example only; check against current BNF/Palliative Care Formulary)?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous morphine is approximately twice as potent as oral, so divide by 2: 150 / 2 = 75 mg over 24 hours. Conversions are approximate, and the plan needs review and verification against current references, particularly in renal impairment.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man with an estimated GFR of 18 mL/min/1.73 m2 and cancer pain is on oral morphine and becoming drowsy with myoclonic jerks. What is the best action?

options.text: Suspect accumulation of morphine metabolites and seek specialist advice about switching to an opioid suited to renal impairment, such as alfentanil or cautious oxycodone
Increase the morphine dose to treat the myoclonus
Stop all analgesia abruptly
Add a benzodiazepine alone and continue the same dose

questions.correctOptionText: Suspect accumulation of morphine metabolites and seek specialist advice about switching to an opioid suited to renal impairment, such as alfentanil or cautious oxycodone

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it recognises toxicity and renal handling and seeks specialist advice.
distractorRationale.b: Increasing the dose would worsen toxicity.
distractorRationale.c: Stopping all analgesia leaves pain uncontrolled; a planned change is needed.
distractorRationale.d: This masks the problem without addressing accumulation.

questions.explanation: Morphine metabolites accumulate in renal impairment, causing sedation and myoclonus. A change to a more suitable opioid should follow specialist or Palliative Care Formulary advice, with an approximate conversion and close monitoring because cross-tolerance is incomplete.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced gastric cancer has early satiety, a sense of fullness and nausea relieved by vomiting. There is no mechanical obstruction. Which antiemetic is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Cyclizine
Haloperidol
Ondansetron
Metoclopramide, a prokinetic

distractorRationale.a: Cyclizine is aimed at vestibular or raised-intracranial-pressure mechanisms.
distractorRationale.b: Haloperidol is aimed at chemical or metabolic causes.
distractorRationale.c: Ondansetron is aimed at serotonin-mediated nausea and tends to cause constipation.

questions.explanation: Early satiety and fullness suggest gastric stasis, for which a prokinetic is appropriate if there is no complete mechanical obstruction. The choice and dose should be confirmed with the current BNF and Palliative Care Formulary.

questions.stem: Which is the best initial approach for chronic breathlessness in an advanced lung disease patient whose oxygen saturation is normal at rest?

options.text: Continuous oxygen for all patients
Non-drug measures such as a handheld fan, positioning and breathing control, with reversible causes treated and drugs considered if needed
Sedation with high-dose benzodiazepines
Reassure the patient that nothing can be done

questions.correctOptionText: Non-drug measures such as a handheld fan, positioning and breathing control, with reversible causes treated and drugs considered if needed

distractorRationale.a: Oxygen is for hypoxaemia, not routinely for breathlessness without it.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it uses first-line, safe measures and addresses causes.
distractorRationale.c: High-dose sedatives carry risk and are not first-line.

questions.explanation: Non-drug measures and treating reversible causes are first-line, followed by symptom-directed drugs such as low-dose opioid, with doses taken from current references. Oxygen is used when hypoxaemia is documented.

questions.stem: A dying patient becomes restless and agitated. Which should be considered before giving a sedative?

options.text: Giving a sedative first, then looking for causes if it fails
Stopping all analgesia
Whether the ward is busy that evening
Reversible causes such as urinary retention, constipation, pain and drug effects

questions.correctOptionText: Reversible causes such as urinary retention, constipation, pain and drug effects

distractorRationale.a: Sedating first can mask a treatable cause and delay its treatment.
distractorRationale.b: Withdrawing analgesia could worsen pain and agitation.
distractorRationale.c: Workload is not a clinical reason to delay assessment.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: reversible contributors are common and treatable.

questions.explanation: Terminal agitation often has treatable contributors such as a full bladder, faecal loading, pain or drug toxicity. Treating these may avoid sedatives, and any drug used is chosen and dosed using current references.

questions.stem: A patient with myeloma is drowsy and constipated. Her measured calcium is 2.88 mmol/L and albumin is 26 g/L. Using adjusted calcium = measured calcium + 0.02 x (40 - albumin in g/L), calculate the albumin-adjusted calcium in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: The albumin difference is 40 - 26 = 14 g/L, and 0.02 x 14 = 0.28 mmol/L, so adjusted calcium is 2.88 + 0.28 = 3.16 mmol/L. This is above the usual reference interval (which varies by laboratory), supporting hypercalcaemia as a cause of her drowsiness and constipation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has had thoracic back pain for a week, now worse lying flat, with new leg weakness and urinary hesitancy. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Reassure and review in a month
Treat as suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with urgent specialist contact and whole-spine MRI, analgesia and corticosteroid according to local protocol
Order a routine outpatient lumbar spine X-ray
Start an oral NSAID and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Treat as suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with urgent specialist contact and whole-spine MRI, analgesia and corticosteroid according to local protocol

distractorRationale.b: Correct: these are red flags needing urgent assessment.
distractorRationale.c: A routine X-ray is not an adequate or timely investigation.

questions.explanation: Back pain in a patient with cancer plus neurological symptoms suggests MSCC, an emergency in which early treatment preserves mobility and continence. Management follows NICE guidance and local protocols.

questions.stem: Describe the principles of titrating strong opioid analgesia for cancer pain in an older adult, including breakthrough dosing, safety measures and the effect of renal impairment.
markingGuide: Assess the pain mechanism and severity, and agree goals with the patient
Start low with oral morphine (modified-release or titrated immediate-release) in older adults, with immediate-release breakthrough doses
Breakthrough dose about one-sixth of the 24-hour total, range one-tenth to one-sixth, hedged and checked against local guidance
Titrate the regular dose according to 24-hour use and review within a day or two
Prescribe a regular laxative and an antiemetic as needed, and monitor for sedation and toxicity
Morphine metabolites accumulate in renal impairment, so seek specialist advice and consider alternatives such as alfentanil or oxycodone
Opioid switching conversions are approximate because cross-tolerance is incomplete; double-check calculations and doses against the BNF and Palliative Care Formulary
questions.explanation: Safe titration uses patient-specific assessment, structured dosing based on actual use, active prevention of side effects and extra care in renal impairment. Calculations and references must be verified.
